message.content: I want to create a global alias for Claude Code and Codex. For Claude Code, I want to be able to just type in cc and have it launch Claude Code in bypass permission mode, and then I want to type in cx and have it launch Codex in Yolo mode.

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

content.text:
Yes. It is already built in. No change needed.

**In VS Code (macOS defaults)**

| Keys | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl` + `` ` `` | Show or hide the terminal panel |
| `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `` ` `` | Open a **new** terminal |
| `Cmd` + `\` | Split the terminal side by side |

Note the modifier is `Ctrl`, not `Cmd`. That is correct on a Mac for these two.

Each new one starts a fresh tmux session, because you just made tmux the default.

**Cheaper option: stay inside tmux**

Once you are in a tmux terminal, you do not need VS Code at all:

- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `c` — new tmux window
- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `n` — next window
- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `p` — previous window

`Ctrl` + `b` is the tmux "prefix". You press it, let go, then press the next key.

**Which I'd use:** the tmux keys. They keep everything in one session, so you can detach and come back later with all your terminals still running. `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `` ` `` makes a brand new session every time, and those pile up.

=== VAULT CLAUDE.md ===
# SecondBrain Vault — Conventions

Writing-and-synthesis vault. Plain markdown, no plugin dependencies. See
`README.md` for the folder philosophy and pilot history.

## Folder semantics (who writes where)

| Folder | Contains | Written by |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| `Inbox/` | Raw capture: interview transcripts, synced meetings, weekly reviews. Cooling-off zone — nothing lives here permanently. | `interview-me`, `meeting-sync`, `weekly-review`, graphify |
| `Notes/` | Atomic permanent notes, one idea per file. | `interview-me` (0–3 per day, only when earned) |
| `Knowledge/` | Evergreen reference. Two kinds: **ingested** external resources (articles, books, frameworks) and **harvested** lesson articles from shipped work. Sub-segmented — see below. | `ingest-resource`, `ingest-book`, `/harvest` |
| `Projects/` | Fuel for active work — research, assets, graphify output, project meetings. | `ingest-resource`, graphify, `meeting-sync` |
| `output/` | `_ledger.md` — running record of shipped artifacts. | `/harvest`, by hand |
| `Drafts/` | Essays/talks-in-progress assembled from linked Notes. | by hand |
| `Archive/` | Published/shipped writing, out of active surface. | by hand |

## Knowledge sub-segmentation

`Knowledge/` root should stay empty — every note lands in a subfolder. Segmented
2026-07-27 because 44 loose files spanned two unrelated domains, so a work query
swept 29 sermon notes it could never use.

| Subfolder | Contains |
|---|---|
| `faith/` | Sermons, church gatherings, biblical study, spiritual formation |
| `sport-science/` | Training methodology, GPS/force-plate references, injury frameworks, cited papers |
| `career-strategy/` | Career positioning, research strategy, interview debriefs |
| `library/` | Advisor book library (`ingest-book`) |
| `frameworks/`, `coaching-frameworks/` | Named frameworks kept as standalone reference |

Routing rule is unchanged — **shelf life decides `Knowledge/` vs `Projects/`**;
these subfolders only decide *where inside* `Knowledge/`. Add a subfolder rather
than dropping a file at the root.

## Archive

`Archive/interviews/` holds daily interview transcripts older than ~30 days.
`Inbox/` says nothing lives there permanently, so transcripts move here once
their content has been distilled into `Notes/`. Wikilinks still resolve —
Obsidian matches `[[2026-06-04-interview]]` by filename regardless of folder.

## The harvest rule

Evergreen **lesson articles** in `Knowledge/` are written ONLY after something
ships — harvested from finished projects via `/harvest`, never speculatively.
(Ingesting *external* reference material via `ingest-resource`/`ingest-book`
is exempt: that's filing someone else's evergreen content, not writing your own.)

## File conventions

- **Filenames:** kebab-case slug of the title (`adoption-is-the-bottleneck.md`).
- **Never overwrite** an existing note. Slug collision → append `-2` or ask to merge.
- **Frontmatter** on every generated note: `type` (resource | harvest | note |
  ledger), `created` (YYYY-MM-DD), `source`, `domain: []`, `tags: []`, `status`.
- **Wikilinks:** link the first mention of any concept/person/project that has
  an existing note. Related-but-unmentioned notes go in a `## Related` section
  (2–5 links max). Links to not-yet-existing notes are allowed sparingly for
  concepts worth a future note.
- **Route by shelf life, not topic:** still true in a year → `Knowledge/`;
  fuel for current work → `Projects/`. Raw capture only ever enters via `Inbox/`.

## Git

The vault is backed up to GitHub (`erash11/SecondBrain`). Commits are backup
artifacts, not reviewed code — commit generated/updated notes with a short
message; don't leave vault changes uncommitted at the end of a session.

# SecondBrain Vault — Conventions

Writing-and-synthesis vault. Plain markdown, no plugin dependencies. See
`README.md` for the folder philosophy and pilot history.

## Folder semantics (who writes where)

| Folder | Contains | Written by |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| `Inbox/` | Raw capture: interview transcripts, synced meetings, weekly reviews. Cooling-off zone — nothing lives here permanently. | `interview-me`, `meeting-sync`, `weekly-review`, graphify |
| `Notes/` | Atomic permanent notes, one idea per file. | `interview-me` (0–3 per day, only when earned) |
| `Knowledge/` | Evergreen reference. Two kinds: **ingested** external resources (articles, books, frameworks) and **harvested** lesson articles from shipped work. Sub-segmented — see below. | `ingest-resource`, `ingest-book`, `/harvest` |
| `Projects/` | Fuel for active work — research, assets, graphify output, project meetings. | `ingest-resource`, graphify, `meeting-sync` |
| `output/` | `_ledger.md` — running record of shipped artifacts. | `/harvest`, by hand |
| `Drafts/` | Essays/talks-in-progress assembled from linked Notes. | by hand |
| `Archive/` | Published/shipped writing, out of active surface. | by hand |

## Knowledge sub-segmentation

`Knowledge/` root should stay empty — every note lands in a subfolder. Segmented
2026-07-27 because 44 loose files spanned two unrelated domains, so a work query
swept 29 sermon notes it could never use.

| Subfolder | Contains |
|---|---|
| `faith/` | Sermons, church gatherings, biblical study, spiritual formation |
| `sport-science/` | Training methodology, GPS/force-plate references, injury frameworks, cited papers |
| `career-strategy/` | Career positioning, research strategy, interview debriefs |
| `library/` | Advisor book library (`ingest-book`) |
| `frameworks/`, `coaching-frameworks/` | Named frameworks kept as standalone reference |

Routing rule is unchanged — **shelf life decides `Knowledge/` vs `Projects/`**;
these subfolders only decide *where inside* `Knowledge/`. Add a subfolder rather
than dropping a file at the root.

## Archive

`Archive/interviews/` holds daily interview transcripts older than ~30 days.
`Inbox/` says nothing lives there permanently, so transcripts move here once
their content has been distilled into `Notes/`. Wikilinks still resolve —
Obsidian matches `[[2026-06-04-interview]]` by filename regardless of folder.

## The harvest rule

Evergreen **lesson articles** in `Knowledge/` are written ONLY after something
ships — harvested from finished projects via `/harvest`, never speculatively.
(Ingesting *external* reference material via `ingest-resource`/`ingest-book`
is exempt: that's filing someone else's evergreen content, not writing your own.)

## File conventions

- **Filenames:** kebab-case slug of the title (`adoption-is-the-bottleneck.md`).
- **Never overwrite** an existing note. Slug collision → append `-2` or ask to merge.
- **Frontmatter** on every generated note: `type` (resource | harvest | note |
  ledger), `created` (YYYY-MM-DD), `source`, `domain: []`, `tags: []`, `status`.
- **Wikilinks:** link the first mention of any concept/person/project that has
  an existing note. Related-but-unmentioned notes go in a `## Related` section
  (2–5 links max). Links to not-yet-existing notes are allowed sparingly for
  concepts worth a future note.
- **Route by shelf life, not topic:** still true in a year → `Knowledge/`;
  fuel for current work → `Projects/`. Raw capture only ever enters via `Inbox/`.

## Git

The vault is backed up to GitHub (`erash11/SecondBrain`). Commits are backup
artifacts, not reviewed code — commit generated/updated notes with a short
message; don't leave vault changes uncommitted at the end of a session.

# tmux Cheat Sheet

> **Summary** — tmux keeps terminal sessions alive after you close the window,
> and splits one window into many panes. Every command starts with the *prefix*:
> press `Ctrl` + `b`, let go, then press the next key. Local install is
> `/opt/homebrew/bin/tmux` (3.7b) running the stock config, so the prefix is the
> default `Ctrl` + `b`. As of 2026-09-04 tmux is the default VS Code terminal
> profile on this Mac.

## The one idea

Three nested things, biggest first:

| Level | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Session** | A whole workspace. Survives closing the terminal. |
| **Window** | A tab inside a session. |
| **Pane** | A split inside a window. |

Detach from a session and it keeps running. Come back later and everything is
where you left it. That is the whole reason to use tmux.

## Sessions

Run these from a normal shell, not inside tmux.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `tmux` | Start a new unnamed session |
| `tmux new -s work` | Start a session named `work` |
| `tmux ls` | List all sessions |
| `tmux attach -t work` | Re-enter the `work` session |
| `tmux new -A -s work` | Attach to `work`, or create it if missing |
| `tmux kill-session -t work` | End the `work` session |
| `tmux kill-server` | End every session |

## Prefix keys

Press `Ctrl` + `b`, release, then the key.

### Session control

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `d` | Detach. Session keeps running in the background. |
| `s` | Pick a session from a list |
| `$` | Rename this session |

### Windows (tabs)

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `c` | New window |
| `n` | Next window |
| `p` | Previous window |
| `0`–`9` | Jump to window by number |
| `w` | Pick a window from a list |
| `,` | Rename this window |
| `&` | Close this window (asks first) |

### Panes (splits)

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `%` | Split left/right |
| `"` | Split top/bottom |
| arrow key | Move to the pane in that direction |
| `o` | Cycle to the next pane |
| `z` | Zoom this pane full screen. Press again to undo. |
| `x` | Close this pane (asks first) |
| `Ctrl` + arrow | Resize the pane |
| `{` / `}` | Swap this pane with the one before/after |
| `!` | Break this pane out into its own window |

### Copy and scroll

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `[` | Enter scroll mode. Arrows / `PgUp` to scroll. `q` to quit. |
| `Space` | (in scroll mode) start selecting |
| `Enter` | (in scroll mode) copy the selection |
| `]` | Paste what you copied |

### Help

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `?` | List every key binding |
| `:` | Command prompt (type a tmux command by name) |

## Local setup notes

- **VS Code**: tmux is the default terminal profile
  (`terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.osx` in
  `~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/settings.json`). The profile runs
  `tmux new-session`, so `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `` ` `` makes a **brand new session**
  every time. Prefer `Ctrl` + `b`, `c` for a new window inside the session you
  already have — otherwise sessions pile up. Check with `tmux ls`.
- **Plain shell escape hatch**: in the terminal panel, click the `∨` next to `+`
  and pick **zsh**.
- **Aliases still work.** tmux starts your login shell, so `~/.zshrc` loads and
  `cc` (Claude Code, permissions bypassed) and `cx` (Codex, yolo) are available
  inside tmux.
- **No `~/.tmux.conf` exists.** Everything above is stock behaviour. If the
  prefix ever stops being `Ctrl` + `b`, a config file appeared.

## The two things worth remembering

1. `Ctrl` + `b`, `d` to walk away. `tmux attach` to come back.
2. `Ctrl` + `b`, `z` to zoom one pane full screen when a split gets too small.

## Related

Explanation: `> /etc/passwd` (or `: > /etc/passwd`, `echo > /etc/passwd`, etc.) opens the target file with O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC — the contents are destroyed before any write happens. This applies equally to `>|` (force-overwrite), `&>` / `>&` (stdout+stderr to file), and numbered FD forms (`1>`, `2>`, `1>|`, `2>|`). All of these are silent, immediate, irrecoverable.

             Safer alternatives:
             - Use append (`>>`) to preserve existing content: `echo line >> <file>`.
             - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak && echo data > <file>`.
             - For temp scratch: `> /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed.
             - Read redirects (`< <file>`) are not affected — they don't truncate.

Good news: you do **not** have to click out. That is exactly what tmux is for.

**Why it works**

tmux sits *between* your keyboard and Claude Code. It grabs `Ctrl` + `b` first. Claude Code never sees it. So from inside a Claude Code session:

- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `c` → new tmux window (Claude Code keeps running in the old one)
- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `n` / `p` → flip between them
- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `0` / `1` → jump straight to one

Your Claude Code session is not interrupted. It stays alive in its own window.

**Better for your case: split instead of a new window**

- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `%` → shell opens beside Claude Code, both visible
- `Ctrl` + `b`, then arrow key → move between the two
- `Ctrl` + `b`, then `z` → zoom whichever one you're in to full screen, press again to shrink back

**This is what I'd use.** You see Claude Code working and run your own commands at the same time. `z` gives you full screen whenever the split gets cramped.

**One tradeoff to know**

Claude Code has its own `Ctrl` + `b` shortcut. tmux now eats it. To send a real `Ctrl` + `b` through to Claude Code, press `Ctrl` + `b` **twice**. That is already set up — I checked.

I added this to your cheat sheet.

## Step 0 — Setup preflight (runs every `/watch` invocation, silent on success)

**Python interpreter:** every `python3 ...` command in this skill is for macOS/Linux. On **Windows**, substitute `python` — the `python3` command on Windows is the Microsoft Store stub and will not run the script.

On the first `/watch` invocation in a session, use structured preflight so you can detect first-run setup:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py" --json
```

Branch on two fields:

- **`can_proceed: true` and `first_run: false`** → setup is already done (the user may have deliberately skipped a Whisper key — that's allowed). Proceed to Step 1 without comment.
- **`first_run: true`** → genuine first-time setup. Do these in order:
  1. If `missing_binaries` is non-empty, run the installer first (it auto-installs on macOS / prints commands elsewhere — see below) and confirm the binaries land. **Do not skip this and jump to preferences.**
  2. Run the installer once more if needed so it scaffolds `~/.config/watch/.env` (it only writes the template when the file is absent, so let it create the file *before* you write any values into it).
  3. Encourage a Whisper API key and ask the watch-preference questions below, then write the selected values into `~/.config/watch/.env` and set `SETUP_COMPLETE=true`.
- **`can_proceed: false` and `first_run: false`** → setup was finished before but the environment regressed (e.g. `missing_binaries` after an OS change). Run the installer to remediate, then proceed. Don't re-ask preferences.

A missing Whisper key is *encouraged to fix, not required*: on a genuine first run `status` will read `needs_key` even when binaries are present — that's your cue to encourage a key, not a blocker.

On follow-up `/watch` calls in the same session, use the silent check:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py" --check
```

This is a <100ms lookup. Exit 0 means /watch can run — this **includes a user who finished setup without a Whisper key** (keyless is allowed). On exit 0 the script emits **nothing** — proceed to Step 1 without comment. **Do NOT announce "setup is complete" to the user** — they don't need a status message on every turn. The only acceptable user-visible output from Step 0 is when remediation is required.

On non-zero exit, follow the table:

| Exit | Meaning | Action |
|------|---------|--------|
| `2` | Missing binaries (`ffmpeg` / `ffprobe` / `yt-dlp`) | Run installer |
| `3` | Genuine first run with no Whisper API key | Run installer to scaffold `.env`, then encourage a key (the user may decline — proceed with `--no-whisper`) |
| `4` | Both missing | Run installer, then encourage a key |

Exit `3` only fires before the user has completed setup. Once `SETUP_COMPLETE=true` is written, a keyless install returns exit 0 and is never nagged again.

The installer is idempotent — safe to re-run:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py"
```

On macOS with Homebrew, it auto-installs `ffmpeg` and `yt-dlp`. On Linux/Windows, it prints the exact install commands for the user to run. It scaffolds `~/.config/watch/.env` with commented placeholders and default watch settings at `0600` perms.

**If an API key is still missing after install:** use `AskUserQuestion` to ask the user whether they have a Groq API key (preferred — cheaper, faster) or an OpenAI key. Then write it into `~/.config/watch/.env` — set the matching `GROQ_API_KEY=...` or `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` line. If they don't want to set up Whisper, proceed with `--no-whisper` and tell them videos without native captions will come back frames-only.

**First-run watch preference:** after the installer has scaffolded `~/.config/watch/.env`, use `AskUserQuestion` to ask one question:

- Default detail (one dial). Present these as `AskUserQuestion` options in this exact order — lightest to heaviest — and keep `(recommended)` on `balanced` even though it is not first (do **not** reorder to put the recommended option first):
  - `transcript` — no frames at all, transcript only (skips video download when captions exist).
  - `efficient` — fast keyframe pass (cap 50).
  - `balanced` (recommended) — scene-aware frames (cap 100, default).
  - `token-burner` — scene-aware, uncapped (maximum fidelity; high token cost).

Write the answer directly into `~/.config/watch/.env` by setting the bare key on its own line — **no trailing inline comment** (a `# note` after the value can break parsing):

```bash
WATCH_DETAIL=balanced
```

Use the user's selected value. If they skip the question, keep the recommended default. Once dependencies, the API-key choice, and this preference are handled, write or update `SETUP_COMPLETE=true` in the same file. Do not ask this preference question again when `SETUP_COMPLETE=true`.

**Structured mode (optional):** `python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py" --json` emits `{status, can_proceed, first_run, setup_complete, missing_binaries, whisper_backend, has_api_key, config_file, watch_detail, platform}` where `status` is one of `ready | needs_install | needs_key | needs_install_and_key`. `status` describes the *ideal* state (a key is encouraged, so a keyless first run reads `needs_key`); `can_proceed` is the operational gate (binaries present AND a key is set OR setup was already completed). Branch on `can_proceed`/`first_run` to decide whether to run; use `status` to decide what to encourage.

Within a single session, you can skip Step 0 on follow-up `/watch` calls — once `--check` returned 0, nothing about the environment changes between turns.

## When to use

- User pastes a video URL (YouTube, Vimeo, X, TikTok, Twitch clip, most yt-dlp-supported sites) and asks about it.
- User points at a local video file (`.mp4`, `.mov`, `.mkv`, `.webm`, etc.) and asks about it.
- User types `/watch <url-or-path> [question]`.

## Recommended limits

- **Best accuracy: videos under 10 minutes.** Frame coverage scales inversely with duration.
- **Universal rate cap: 2 fps.** The script never samples faster than 2 fps, even when a budget or `--fps` would imply more.
- **The frame ceiling is set by the detail mode** (`WATCH_DETAIL` in `~/.config/watch/.env`, or `--detail`), not a single global cap:
  - `transcript` → no frames
  - `efficient` → up to **50** (keyframes)
  - `balanced` (default) → up to **100** (scene-aware)
  - `token-burner` → **uncapped** (scene-aware; a soft warning prints past 250 frames)
  - `--max-frames N` overrides whichever cap the mode would otherwise use.
- **Full-video frame budget by duration.** Token cost grows with frame count, so the script targets a budget by duration. This budget sets the fps and the uniform-sampling fallback; scene-aware selection can fill up to the detail cap above, whichever is lower:
  - ≤30s → ~12-30 frames
  - 30s-1min → ~40 frames
  - 1-3min → ~60 frames
  - 3-10min → ~80 frames
  - \>10min → up to the detail cap, sparsely spaced (warning printed)
- If the user hands you a long video, consider asking whether they want a specific section before burning tokens on a sparse scan.

## How to invoke

**Step 1 — parse the user input.** Separate the video source (URL or path) from any question the user asked. Example: `/watch https://youtu.be/abc what language is this in?` → source = `https://youtu.be/abc`, question = `what language is this in?`.

**Step 2 — run the watch script.** Pass the source verbatim. Do not shell-escape it yourself beyond normal quoting:

```bash
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" "<source>"
```

Optional flags:
- `--detail transcript|efficient|balanced|token-burner` — fidelity/speed dial. `transcript` = no frames (transcript only, skips video download when captions exist); `efficient` = fast keyframes (cap 50); `balanced` = scene-aware frames (cap 100); `token-burner` = scene-aware, uncapped.
- `--start T` / `--end T` — focus on a section. Accepts `SS`, `MM:SS`, or `HH:MM:SS`. When either is set, fps auto-scales denser (see "Focusing on a section" below).
- `--timestamps T1,T2,…` — grab a frame at each of these absolute timestamps (`SS`, `MM:SS`, or `HH:MM:SS`). Use this after reading the transcript to capture deictic moments the presenter flags ("look here", "as you can see", "notice this") that visual selection alone may miss. See "Transcript-cue frames" below.
- `--max-frames N` — override the preset cap for tighter token budget (e.g. `--max-frames 40`)
- `--resolution W` — change frame width in px (default 512; bump to 1024 only if the user needs to read on-screen text)
- `--fps F` — override auto-fps (clamped to 2 fps max)
- `--out-dir DIR` — keep working files somewhere specific (default: an auto-generated tmp dir)
- `--whisper groq|openai` — force a specific Whisper backend (default: prefer Groq if both keys exist)
- `--no-whisper` — disable the Whisper fallback entirely (frames-only if no captions)
- `--no-dedup` — keep near-duplicate frames. By default a frame-delta pass drops frames that are visually near-identical to the previous kept one (held slides, static screen recordings, paused video) so the frame budget goes to distinct content; the report's **Frames** line notes how many were dropped. Pass this only if the user needs every sampled frame (e.g. judging subtle frame-to-frame motion).

### Focusing on a section (higher frame rate)

When the user asks about a specific moment — "what happens at the 2 minute mark?", "zoom into 0:45 to 1:00", "the first 10 seconds" — pass `--start` and/or `--end`. The script switches to focused-mode budgets, which are denser than full-video budgets (still capped at 2 fps, and still bounded by the detail-mode cap — the counts below assume the default `balanced` cap of 100; `efficient` tops out at 50):

- ≤5s → 2 fps (up to 10 frames)
- 5-15s → 2 fps (up to 30 frames)
- 15-30s → ~2 fps (up to 60 frames)
- 30-60s → ~1.3 fps (up to 80 frames)
- 60-180s → ~0.6 fps (100 frames, capped)

Focused mode is the right call for:
- Any moment/range the user names explicitly ("around 2:30", "the intro", "the last 30 seconds").
- Any video longer than ~10 minutes where the user's question is about a specific part — running focused on the relevant section is far more useful than a sparse scan of the whole thing.
- Re-runs after a full scan didn't have enough detail in some region.

Transcript is auto-filtered to the same range. Frame timestamps are absolute (real video timeline, not offset-from-start).

Examples:
```bash
# Last 10 seconds of a 1 minute video
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" video.mp4 --start 50 --end 60

# Zoom into 2:15 → 2:45 at 2 fps (60 frames)
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" "$URL" --start 2:15 --end 2:45 --fps 2

# From 1h12m to the end of the video
python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.py" "$URL" --start 1:12:00
```

**Step 3 — Read every frame path the script lists.** The Read tool renders JPEGs directly as images for you. Read all frames in a single message (parallel tool calls) so you see them together. The frames are in chronological order with a `t=MM:SS` timestamp so you can align them to the transcript.

**Step 4 — answer the user.** You now have two streams of evidence:
- **Frames** — what's on screen at each timestamp
- **Transcript** — what's said at each timestamp. The report's header shows the source (`captions` = yt-dlp pulled native subs; `whisper (groq)` or `whisper (openai)` = transcribed by API).

If the user asked a specific question, answer it directly citing timestamps. If they didn't ask anything, summarize what happens in the video — structure, key moments, notable visuals, spoken content.

This holds for `transcript` detail too: even with no frames, produce a **summary** like the other modes — do not paste the full transcript into chat. Synthesize structure, key moments, and spoken content with timestamps; quote only the lines that matter. Offer the raw transcript only if the user explicitly asks for it.

**Step 5 — clean up.** The script prints a working directory at the end. If the user isn't going to ask follow-ups about this video, delete it with `rm -rf <dir>`. If they might, leave it in place.

## Detail and frames

Default behavior comes from `~/.config/watch/.env`:

- `WATCH_DETAIL=transcript|efficient|balanced|token-burner` (default: `balanced`)

At `transcript` detail, captions are enough to return a report without downloading video. If captions are missing, the script downloads audio only and tries Whisper. If no transcript can be produced, it reports the limitation clearly; re-run with `--detail balanced` for frames.

At `efficient` detail, the script downloads the video and extracts **keyframes only** (`ffmpeg -skip_frame nokey`) — a near-instant pass that lands frames on scene cuts. If a clip has fewer than 4 keyframes it falls back to uniform sampling.

At `balanced` / `token-burner` detail, the script extracts **scene-aware** frames: ffmpeg scene-change selection first, falling back to uniform sampling only when the video is effectively static. `balanced` caps at 100 frames; `token-burner` is uncapped. Frame report lines include both timestamp and selection reason. Extracted images are clamped to a maximum 1998px height for Claude Read compatibility.

## Transcript-cue frames

Visual frame selection (scene/keyframe) can miss the moments a presenter explicitly flags — "look here", "as you can see", "notice this", "watch what happens" — because pointing at a slide is often a *low* visual change. `--timestamps` lets you force a frame at those exact moments. **You** decide which moments matter, by reading the transcript:

1. Run once at `--detail transcript` (or any detail) to get the timestamped transcript.
2. Scan it for deictic cues — phrases where the speaker directs attention to something on screen. This is a judgment call (ignore rhetorical "look, the point is…"); that's why it's done by you, not a regex.
3. Re-run with `--timestamps 4:32,7:10,9:55` (absolute source times). For a URL, point the second run at the **downloaded local file** in the work dir so it doesn't re-download.

Behavior:
- **Additive by default.** Cue frames (`reason=transcript-cue`) are merged into whatever `--detail` already selected, in chronological order.
- **Pinned and counted first.** Cue frames are reserved against the frame cap before the detail engine runs, so they're never evicted by even-sampling.
- **Honors focus mode.** With `--start/--end`, any cue timestamp outside the window is dropped (reported in the summary). Coordinates are always absolute source time.
- **Cue-only frames.** `--detail transcript --timestamps …` skips scene/keyframe sampling and returns *only* the cue frames (it will download the video to do so, since frames need pixels).

## Transcription

The script gets a timestamped transcript in one of two ways:

1. **Native captions (free, preferred).** yt-dlp pulls manual or auto-generated subtitles from the source platform if available.
2. **Whisper API fallback.** If no captions came back (or the source is a local file), the script extracts audio (`ffmpeg -vn -ac 1 -ar 16000 -b:a 64k`, ~0.5 MB/min) and uploads it to whichever Whisper API has a key configured:
   - **Groq** — `whisper-large-v3`. Preferred default: cheaper, faster. Get a key at console.groq.com/keys.
   - **OpenAI** — `whisper-1`. Fallback. Get a key at platform.openai.com/api-keys.

Both keys live in `~/.config/watch/.env`. The script prefers Groq when both are set; override with `--whisper openai` to force OpenAI. Use `--no-whisper` to skip the fallback entirely.

## Failure modes and handling

- **Setup preflight failed** → run `python3 "${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/setup.py"` (auto-installs ffmpeg/yt-dlp via brew on macOS, scaffolds the `.env`). For API key, ask the user via `AskUserQuestion` and write it to `~/.config/watch/.env`.
- **No transcript available** → captions missing AND (no Whisper key OR Whisper API failed). Script prints a hint pointing to setup. Proceed frames-only and tell the user.
- **Long video warning printed** → acknowledge it in your answer. Offer to re-run focused on a specific section via `--start`/`--end` rather than a sparse full-video scan.
- **Download fails** → yt-dlp's error goes to stderr. If it's a login-required or region-locked video, tell the user plainly; do not keep retrying.
- **Whisper request fails** → the error is printed to stderr (likely: invalid key or rate limit). Audio over the API's 25 MB upload cap is split into chunks and transcribed automatically, so length alone won't fail it; if some chunks fail the transcript is partial and the dropped chunks are noted on stderr. The report will say "none available" only if every chunk fails. You can retry with `--whisper openai` if Groq failed (or vice versa).

## Token efficiency

This skill burns tokens primarily on frames. Order of magnitude:
- 80 frames at 512px wide is roughly 50-80k image tokens depending on aspect ratio.
- The transcript is cheap (a few thousand tokens at most for a 10-minute video).
- Bumping `--resolution` to 1024 roughly quadruples the image tokens per frame. Only do it when necessary.

If you already watched a video this session and the user asks a follow-up, do **not** re-run the script — you already have the frames and transcript in context. Just answer from what you have.

## Security & Permissions

**What this skill does:**
- Runs `yt-dlp` locally to download the video and pull native captions when the source supports them (public data; the request goes directly to whatever host the URL points at)
- Runs `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe` locally to extract frames as JPEGs and, when Whisper is needed, a mono 16 kHz audio clip
- Sends the extracted audio clip to Groq's Whisper API (`api.groq.com/openai/v1/audio/transcriptions`) when `GROQ_API_KEY` is set (preferred — cheaper, faster)
- Sends the extracted audio clip to OpenAI's audio transcription API (`api.openai.com/v1/audio/transcriptions`) when `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set and Groq is not, or when `--whisper openai` is forced
- Writes the downloaded video, frames, audio, and an intermediate transcript to a working directory under the system temp dir (or `--out-dir` if specified) so Claude can `Read` them
- Reads / creates `~/.config/watch/.env` (mode `0600`) to store the Whisper API key(s) and a `SETUP_COMPLETE` marker. As a fallback, also reads `.env` in the current working directory

**What this skill does NOT do:**
- Does not upload the video itself to any API — only the extracted audio goes out, and only when native captions are missing AND Whisper is not disabled with `--no-whisper`
- Does not access any platform account (no login, no session cookies, no posting) — yt-dlp only ever requests public data
- Does not share API keys between providers (Groq key only goes to `api.groq.com`, OpenAI key only goes to `api.openai.com`)
- Does not log, cache, or write API keys to stdout, stderr, or output files
- Does not persist anything outside the working directory and `~/.config/watch/.env` — clean up the working directory when you're done (Step 5)

**Bundled scripts:** `scripts/watch.py` (entry point), `scripts/download.py` (yt-dlp wrapper), `scripts/frames.py` (ffmpeg frame extraction), `scripts/transcribe.py` (caption selection + Whisper orchestration), `scripts/whisper.py` (Groq / OpenAI clients), `scripts/setup.py` (preflight + installer)

content.text:
## Part 1 — I found your problem

You have **7 separate tmux sessions** running, each with one lonely pane:

```
0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6   ← all created in the last 15 minutes
```

Every time you clicked `+`, VS Code ran `tmux new-session`. That makes a **brand new session**, not a split. That's why nothing ever appeared side by side.

**I just split your active window from here.** Look at your terminal — a second pane should have appeared on the right, with a message in it. If you see it, tmux splitting works fine and the `+` button was the problem all along.

### What to actually do

Stop using the `+` button. Use **one** tmux terminal and split inside it:

| Keys | Result |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl` + `b`, then `%` | Split side by side ← **this is what you want** |
| `Ctrl` + `b`, then `"` | Split top and bottom |
| `Ctrl` + `b`, then arrow | Jump between panes |
| `Ctrl` + `b`, then `z` | Zoom one pane full screen |

So: left pane run `cc`, right pane run `cx`. Both visible.

**Clean up the junk sessions** when you're ready:

```
tmux kill-session -t 1; tmux kill-session -t 4; tmux kill-session -t 6
```

(I left 2, 3, 5 alone — they show as attached, so something may be using them. Run `tmux ls` to check.)

---

## Part 2 — The video

**"My Agentic Engineering Workflow (after 6,775 sessions)" — David Ondrej, 54 min.**

**Be warned:** roughly 10 minutes of it (10:00–20:00 and the outro) is a paid Hostinger ad. He tells you to buy a VPS. **Skip that.** Your own CLAUDE.md says no cloud servers without Baylor IT approval. That whole section is closed to you for work.

### What you already have

At **25:41** — the exact spot you linked — he says: make a global alias `cc` for Claude Code and `cx` for Codex. **Done, an hour ago.** That's where you got the idea.

At **34:36** he calls guardrail hooks "absolutely non-negotiable — never use YOLO mode without this." **You already have this.** It's called `dcg`. It blocked me earlier today when I tried to overwrite a file in your home folder. It worked exactly as designed.

So you are ahead of the video on the two things it calls essential.

### Four things worth stealing

**1. Voice dictation** (14:04). You type ~40–80 words/min. You speak ~250. He uses SuperWhisper. This is the single biggest speed gain in the video and it costs you nothing to try.

**2. Text snippets** (27:36). He keeps canned prompts on hotkeys — "be concise", "make that shorter", "execute the plan fully". macOS Text Replacement does this for free. Raycast is faster.

**3. Ask before build** (30:14). Before a big change, make the agent list the 3–5 real decisions and *you* pick. His line: models are good at implementation, bad at judgment. That matches how you already work.

**4. Review once, not in a loop** (42:33). Build with one model, review with a different one, fix the top issues, ship. Do **not** review the review. His warning: models will invent fake bugs forever rather than say "this is fine."

### What to ignore

- **The VPS section.** Sponsored, and blocked for you anyway.
- **Worktrees.** He says himself: only worth it past 15 parallel agents. You are not there.
- **Buying four subscriptions.** He's optimizing for a job you don't have.
- **"BB", "cmux", "herder", "Pi".** Tool churn. He says outright the video will be outdated in a month.

---

## Is your setup good?

You asked honestly, so: **yes, and the video does not argue otherwise.**

You have the aliases. You have the guardrail hook. You have tmux for persistence. That is the whole local stack the video actually recommends. Everything else in it is either an ad or built for someone running 30 agents at once.

**The one real gap is voice dictation.** Want me to look at what's involved in setting that up?

10	# tmux Cheat Sheet
11	
12	> **Summary** — tmux keeps terminal sessions alive after you close the window,
13	> and splits one window into many panes. Every command starts with the *prefix*:
14	> press `Ctrl` + `b`, let go, then press the next key. Local install is

17	> profile on this Mac.
18	
19	## The one idea
20	
21	Three nested things, biggest first:
22	
23	| Level | What it is |
24	|---|---|
25	| **Session** | A whole workspace. Survives closing the terminal. |
26	| **Window** | A tab inside a session. |
27	| **Pane** | A split inside a window. |
28	
29	Detach from a session and it keeps running. Come back later and everything is
30	where you left it. That is the whole reason to use tmux.
31	
32	## Sessions
33	
34	Run these from a normal shell, not inside tmux.
35	
36	| Command | What it does |
37	|---|---|
38	| `tmux` | Start a new unnamed session |
39	| `tmux new -s work` | Start a session named `work` |
40	| `tmux ls` | List all sessions |
41	| `tmux attach -t work` | Re-enter the `work` session |
42	| `tmux new -A -s work` | Attach to `work`, or create it if missing |
43	| `tmux kill-session -t work` | End the `work` session |
44	| `tmux kill-server` | End every session |
45	
46	## Prefix keys
47	
48	Press `Ctrl` + `b`, **release both keys**, then press the next key on its own.
49	Holding `Ctrl` down for the second key sends a different signal — `Ctrl` + `b`
50	then `Ctrl` + `c` interrupts the running program instead of making a window.
51	
52	### Session control
53	
54	| Key | What it does |
55	|---|---|
56	| `d` | Detach. Session keeps running in the background. |
57	| `s` | Pick a session from a list |
58	| `$` | Rename this session |
59	
60	### Windows (tabs)
61	
62	| Key | What it does |
63	|---|---|
64	| `c` | New window |
65	| `n` | Next window |
66	| `p` | Previous window |
67	| `0`–`9` | Jump to window by number |
68	| `w` | Pick a window from a list |
69	| `,` | Rename this window |
70	| `&` | Close this window (asks first) |
71	
72	### Panes (splits)
73	
74	| Key | What it does |
75	|---|---|
76	| `%` | Split left/right |
77	| `"` | Split top/bottom |
78	| arrow key | Move to the pane in that direction |
79	| `o` | Cycle to the next pane |
80	| `z` | Zoom this pane full screen. Press again to undo. |
81	| `x` | Close this pane (asks first) |
82	| `Ctrl` + arrow | Resize the pane |
83	| mouse click | Focus a pane (needs `set -g mouse on`) |
84	| `{` / `}` | Swap this pane with the one before/after |
85	| `!` | Break this pane out into its own window |
86	
87	### Copy and scroll
88	
89	| Key | What it does |
90	|---|---|
91	| `[` | Enter scroll mode. Arrows / `PgUp` to scroll. `q` to quit. |
92	| `Space` | (in scroll mode) start selecting |
93	| `Enter` | (in scroll mode) copy the selection |
94	| `]` | Paste what you copied |
95	
96	### Help
97	
98	| Key | What it does |
99	|---|---|
100	| `?` | List every key binding |
101	| `:` | Command prompt (type a tmux command by name) |
102	
103	## Running Claude Code inside tmux
104	
105	tmux sits between the keyboard and whatever runs in the pane, so it takes the
106	prefix **before** Claude Code sees it. Every key below works without leaving or
107	interrupting a live Claude Code session.
108	
109	| Keys | What it does |
110	|---|---|
111	| `Ctrl` + `b`, `%` | Open a shell beside Claude Code. Both stay visible. |
112	| `Ctrl` + `b`, arrow | Move between Claude Code and the shell |
113	| `Ctrl` + `b`, `z` | Zoom the focused pane full screen. Press again to shrink. |
114	| `Ctrl` + `b`, `c` | New window instead of a split. Claude Code keeps running behind it. |
115	| `Ctrl` + `b`, `n` / `p` | Flip between windows |
116	
117	Splitting beats a new window here: Claude Code stays in sight while you work,
118	and `z` gives full screen on demand.
119	
120	**The one clash.** Claude Code binds `Ctrl` + `b` itself, and tmux now swallows
121	it. Press `Ctrl` + `b` **twice** to pass a literal `Ctrl` + `b` through to the
122	app. Stock tmux already binds this (`bind-key -T prefix C-b send-prefix`).
123	
124	## The mouse does nothing by default
125	
126	Stock tmux ignores the mouse entirely — clicking another pane will not move
127	focus, and the scroll wheel scrolls the shell's own history rather than tmux's.

130	```

135	so `Cmd` + `C` no longer copies the selection. Hold `Option` while dragging to
136	get a normal terminal selection.
137

142	1. **Are you actually in tmux?** Run `echo $TMUX`. Empty output means you are

144	2. **Did you release `Ctrl`?** See the note above the tables.
145	3. **Is something eating the key?** In a tmux pane run

148	   `tmux new-window`. If the command works but the key does not, the key is

159	   set -g prefix C-a

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence (commit+push to KeystoneOS is standing-authorized per `feedback-auto-commit-push`; for any OTHER repo with changes, commit locally and list the push as an open item instead of pushing).

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- KeystoneOS: stage, commit with a descriptive message, push. Authorized.
- Other repos with changes: commit locally with a descriptive message; do NOT push without asking — list it in the final report instead.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Never push to a repo other than KeystoneOS without explicit approval.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff — 2026-09-04 — Terminal + agent launcher setup

## What this session was

Eric wanted one-keystroke launchers for his two coding agents, then kept pulling
the thread: tmux as the VS Code terminal, side-by-side panes so Claude Code and
Codex are visible at once, and a written reference in the vault. Prompted by
David Ondrej's video "My Agentic Engineering Workflow (after 6,775 sessions)"
(YouTube `c9nRxEy1kUY`, 54:20) — specifically the 25:41 mark, where he
recommends exactly the `cc` / `cx` aliases.

## What changed

| Path | Change |
|---|---|
| `~/.zshrc` (lines 54–55) | `cc` → `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`; `cx` → `codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. **Pre-existed** this session under an "agent launchers (added 2026-09-04)" block — verified working, not re-added. |
| `~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/settings.json` | Added `terminal.integrated.profiles.osx` (a `tmux` profile running `/opt/homebrew/bin/tmux new-session`, plus a `zsh` escape-hatch profile) and `terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.osx: "tmux"`. Backup at `settings.json.bak` in the same folder. |
| `~/.tmux.conf` | **Created.** `mouse on`, `history-limit 50000`, `base-index 1` + `renumber-windows on`, splits/new-windows inherit `pane_current_path`, `prefix r` reloads. Prefix deliberately left at stock `Ctrl+b`. |
| `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/tooling/tmux-cheat-sheet.md` | **Created**, plus a new `Knowledge/tooling/` subfolder. 4 commits: `87bbb52`, `136b712`, `c543a73`, `9d859a3`. |

## Decisions and the reasoning behind them

- **`Knowledge/tooling/` is a new vault subfolder.** None of the existing ones
  (faith, sport-science, career-strategy, library, frameworks,
  coaching-frameworks) fit a CLI reference, and the vault's `CLAUDE.md` says to
  add a subfolder rather than drop a file at `Knowledge/` root.
- **tmux prefix stays `Ctrl+b`.** No clash was found — `terminal.integrated.commandsToSkipShell`
  in the VS Code settings already carries `-workbench.action.toggleSidebarVisibility`,
  which hands `Ctrl+b` back to the shell. Changing the prefix would have made
  every tutorial and the cheat sheet wrong for no gain.
- **The VS Code profile runs bare `tmux new-session`, not `new-session -A -s main`.**
  `-A` would have made every VS Code terminal attach to one shared session, and
  multiple clients on one session *mirror* each other — confusing. The cost is
  that the `+` button spawns a fresh session each time, which is documented in
  the cheat sheet with the instruction to split inside one session instead.
- **Did not push the vault.** Standing rule: only KeystoneOS is push-authorized.

## Two real bugs found and fixed

1. **"`Ctrl+b c` doesn't work."** Root cause: he had **7 stray tmux sessions**,
   each with one pane, because every `+` click ran `tmux new-session`. Splits
   were working; he was making new sessions instead of splitting.
2. **"I couldn't click back into the other panel."** Root cause: stock tmux
   ignores the mouse entirely. Fixed by `set -g mouse on` in the new
   `~/.tmux.conf`. Documented tradeoff: with mouse on, hold **Option** while
   dragging to get a selection macOS `Cmd+C` can copy.

## Video triage (so nobody re-watches 54 minutes)

Full deduped transcript was pulled but lives in job-temp and will not survive.
The filtered verdict:

- **Already had:** the `cc`/`cx` aliases (25:41) and the guardrail pre-tool hook
  (34:36, which the video calls non-negotiable) — that is `dcg`, and it fired
  correctly during this session, blocking a truncating redirect into `$HOME`.
  Voice dictation (14:04) — Eric confirmed he already has it.
- **Worth stealing:** text snippets for repeated prompts (27:36); "ask before
  build" — make the agent surface 3–5 decisions before a big change (30:14);
  review once with a *different* model, never recursively (42:33); tell models
  explicitly to stop adding tests (48:37).
- **Ignore:** the 10:00–20:00 VPS section is a **paid Hostinger ad**, and cloud
  servers are blocked for Eric's work anyway (no cloud without Baylor IT
  approval). Worktrees — the video itself says they only pay off past ~15
  parallel agents. Buying four AI subscriptions. The tool-of-the-week names
  (BB, cmux, herder, Pi); the presenter says the video is stale in a month.

## Next actions

1. **Push the vault** — 4 commits sit unpushed on `~/SecondBrain` (`erash11/SecondBrain`).
   Not done because only KeystoneOS is push-authorized.
2. **Clean up stray tmux sessions.** `tmux ls` showed 7. Sessions 1, 4, 6 were
   idle and empty: `tmux kill-session -t 1; tmux kill-session -t 4; tmux kill-session -t 6`.
   2, 3, 5 showed as attached — check before killing.
3. **Close the demo pane** left in session `0:0` — `Ctrl+b` then `x`. It was
   created deliberately to prove splitting worked.

## Mid-flight / open

Nothing blocking. Eric said "I'm not sure this is the best setup, still trying
to figure a lot of this out" — the honest read given to him was that his local
stack (aliases + guardrail hook + tmux + voice) already matches everything the
video actually recommends for someone not running 30 parallel agents, and the
remainder of the video is sponsorship or scale he does not have.
